newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica companies worry on state of nation.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica companies worry on state of nation.

text.p: Corporate South Africa is worried -- and the picture of Pepkor Chairman Christo Wiese in his latest annual report tells it all.
Instead of the usual urbane, smiling full-colour portrait on glossy paper, there is a grainy, sepia picture of a frowning Wiese, hand on chin and looking down at papers on his desk.

The Cape-based retailing group's financial results don't warrant such a pose, but it reflects a growing concern about the state of the nation half-way through the first term of government in the new South African democracy.
"The euphoria which initially pervaded the business community after 1994 has made way for considerable disillusionment," Wiese said in his annual review alongside his sombre portrait.

The extent of that disillusionment was further highlighted recently when Sappi Saiccor Managing Director Roland Mazery said he was backing an international campaign to draw attention to South Africa's escalating crime rate.

Acting in his personal capacity, Mazery has been bombarding foreign investors, diplomats and officials with letters and negative press clippings in a bid to force the government to take stronger action on crime.
The move has been denounced by government, unions and Business Against Crime, but Mazery claims he has been inundated with congratulatory calls from the public.
Woolworths (South Africa) Chairman Colin Hall tackles the problem differently in his latest annual report.

"We actively promote the idea of merging all the armed manpower available, including the many thousands employed by the private sector, into a single cohesive 'force for the security of all citizens' - a peace corps."
If adequately armed, this would restore peace and stability for all South Africans and their property, he said.
But Hall, Wiese and other leading businessmen have other concerns apart from crime.
"Many and diverse matters cause disquiet," Wiese said.

These included indecision about the scrapping of exchange controls, the outflow of skilled whites from the civil service as affirmative action is implemented, and the unwillingness of government to rein in the trade unions.

The outflow of skilled staff has been blamed for the virtual breakdown of customs inspection at the country's ports, which has led to a flood of illegal imports. Worst affected have been the clothing and textiles industries, which cannot compete with cheap imports from the Far East.

Top executives have, however, given the government full marks for its new economic strategy, which it has said was "non-negotiable" despite union opposition to many elements, including privatisation and tax holidays.
This has been particularly welcomed by business, which has become increasingly frustrated by government's perceived indecision on major issues.
"Good government and the decision making this entails cannot be replaced by transparency consultation and consensus," Wiese said.
"Unfortunately, a culture has developed in South Africa that places a high premium on deliberation and debate, and apparently none on decision-making.

"One can understand the background against which this emphasis on transparency developed, but when consultation and consensus are taken to such extremes that ... decision-making and effective action are impaired, the country pays a very high price."
South Africa had been readmitted to a very competitive international community and to survive needs vision and drive "as well as the willingness to take unpopular decisions if necessary," Wiese said.
Most South Africans still had unrealistic expectations of the new government and it was time they came back to earth and accepted the harsh economic realities of the country, he said.
"One such reality is that South Africa is not a rich country, and that its resources are dwindling," Wiese said.
"Another is that redistribution of the country's modest wealth will not bring prosperity to all. Only hard work will do this."
